source_policy.authority: Supplied source text is authoritative for source-derived claims.
source_policy.preservation_rule: Preserve source terminology, taxonomy, mechanisms, historical sequence, examples, distinctions and references without silently correcting or replacing the source.

central_system_flows: Physical hardware -> hypervisor -> isolated system VM -> guest OS
Host OS -> process VM -> program -> platform-independent execution
Kernel -> OS-level virtualization -> isolated guest environments sharing kernel
Outer hypervisor -> nested VM -> nested hypervisor
Compiler -> intermediate representation -> process VM -> machine architecture

nodes.label: Virtual Machine
nodes.description: Virtualization or emulation of a computer system based on a computer architecture, providing functionality of a physical computer.

nodes.label: System Virtual Machine
nodes.description: Full/system virtualization VM that substitutes for a real machine and can execute an entire operating system.

nodes.label: Process Virtual Machine
nodes.description: VM designed to execute computer programs in a platform-independent environment, normally as a process within a host OS.

nodes.label: Host
nodes.description: Physical or real-world machine running a VM.

nodes.label: Guest
nodes.description: Virtual machine or environment emulated on a host.

nodes.label: Hypervisor
nodes.description: Software layer using native execution to share/manage hardware and isolate multiple environments.

nodes.label: Physical Hardware
nodes.description: Physical computer hardware on which virtualization is implemented.

nodes.label: Host CPU
nodes.description: Processor providing execution resources and, on modern systems, hardware virtualization assistance.

nodes.label: Guest Operating System
nodes.description: Operating system executing inside a system VM.

nodes.label: Host Operating System
nodes.description: Operating system running on the physical host.

nodes.label: Virtual Hardware
nodes.description: Hardware interface presented to a guest VM.

nodes.label: Physical Machine
nodes.description: Real computer corresponding to the physical host.

nodes.label: OS-level Virtualization
nodes.description: Virtualization at operating-system level that partitions resources through the kernel while sharing the host OS kernel.

nodes.label: Full Virtualization
nodes.description: Virtualization providing enough simulated hardware for an unmodified guest OS designed for the same instruction set.

nodes.label: Hardware-Assisted Virtualization
nodes.description: Virtualization using architectural hardware support to facilitate a virtual machine monitor and guest isolation.

nodes.label: Software Virtualization
nodes.description: Virtualization techniques implemented primarily in software.

nodes.label: Virtual Memory
nodes.description: Memory abstraction historically preceding and conceptually generalized by system virtualization.

nodes.label: Time-sharing
nodes.description: Concurrent use of a computer by switching execution among programs/users and saving/restoring state.

nodes.label: Isolation
nodes.description: Separation of VM environments so they can coexist on one physical machine.

nodes.label: Server Consolidation
nodes.description: Use of multiple VMs on one physical machine to consolidate server workloads.

nodes.label: Embedded Systems
nodes.description: Systems where VMs can run multiple operating-system environments, including real-time and complex OSs.

nodes.label: Software Sandbox
nodes.description: Isolation environment for novel, unproven, or risky software.

nodes.label: Process
nodes.description: Running program instance; process VMs support a single process.

nodes.label: Platform Independence
nodes.description: Ability for a program to execute consistently across different underlying hardware/OS environments.

nodes.label: Managed Runtime Environment
nodes.description: Process VM / application VM environment abstracting underlying platform.

nodes.label: Interpreter
nodes.description: Implementation mechanism executing process-VM instructions.

nodes.label: Just-in-time Compilation
nodes.description: Compilation approach that can make interpreted/process-VM execution competitive with compiled performance.

nodes.label: Program
nodes.description: Program executed inside a process VM.

nodes.label: Programming Language
nodes.description: High-level programming language abstracted by a process VM.

nodes.label: Intermediate Representation
nodes.description: Intermediate code representation that process VMs can execute or target.

nodes.label: Machine Code
nodes.description: Native instructions executed by physical hardware.

nodes.label: Instruction Set Architecture
nodes.description: Instruction set architecture defining the machine interface a guest or VM targets.

nodes.label: Computer Cluster
nodes.description: Potentially heterogeneous collection of machines whose communication can be abstracted by a cluster-oriented process VM.

nodes.label: Parallel Virtual Machine
nodes.description: Cluster-oriented virtual-machine system supporting concurrent programming abstraction.

nodes.label: Message Passing Interface
nodes.description: Cluster communication system named as an example of a process-VM-like abstraction.

nodes.label: Unmodified Guest OS
nodes.description: Guest operating system that can execute without modification under full virtualization.

nodes.label: QEMU
nodes.description: Emulator/virtualization software cited as capable of emulating other architectures.

nodes.label: Emulator
nodes.description: Software that imitates a different computer architecture or platform.

nodes.label: VM Snapshot
nodes.description: State of a VM and generally its storage devices at an exact point in time.

nodes.label: Virtual Disk
nodes.description: Virtual disk presented to a VM, potentially backed by a host file.

nodes.label: Snapshot Overlay Layer
nodes.description: Overlay file holding changes after a snapshot.

nodes.label: Snapshot Stack
nodes.description: Hierarchy of snapshot overlays representing a coherent virtual disk.

nodes.label: VM RAM State
nodes.description: RAM contents that can be included in a VM snapshot.

nodes.label: VM BIOS State
nodes.description: BIOS settings that can be included in a VM snapshot.

nodes.label: VM Configuration State
nodes.description: VM configuration settings that can be included in snapshots.

nodes.label: Snapshot Restore
nodes.description: Restoration that discards/ignores overlay layers created after a selected snapshot and redirects new changes.

nodes.label: VM Migration
nodes.description: Moving a VM's snapshot/state to another host/hypervisor and resuming it there.

nodes.label: Service-preserving Migration
nodes.description: Migration performed with regularly synchronized snapshots and brief interruption to support maintenance.

nodes.label: VM Failover
nodes.description: Continuing VM operation after host failure from the last coherent state supplied to a backup server.

nodes.label: Backup Server
nodes.description: Server retaining material needed for VM failover.

nodes.label: Nested Virtualization
nodes.description: Running one or more hypervisors/VMs inside another VM/hypervisor.

nodes.label: Nested Hypervisor
nodes.description: Hypervisor executing inside another hypervisor.

nodes.label: Outer Hypervisor
nodes.description: Hypervisor providing the environment in which a nested hypervisor runs.

nodes.label: Nested Virtualization Hardware Support
nodes.description: Hardware support used to accelerate or enable nested virtualization.

nodes.label: VMCS Shadowing
nodes.description: Intel technology cited as accelerating nested virtualization on Haswell-era processors.

nodes.label: VM Security Isolation
nodes.description: Use of VMs to isolate applications from each other for security.

nodes.label: Malware
nodes.description: Malicious software whose spread can be constrained by compartmentalized VM architectures.

nodes.label: Qubes OS
nodes.description: Operating system architecture using distinct VMs/AppVMs for compartmentalization.

nodes.label: Whonix
nodes.description: Security system listed as using VM-based compartmentalization.

nodes.label: Kicksecure
nodes.description: Security system listed as using VM-based compartmentalization.

nodes.label: Dangerzone
nodes.description: Application/system listed as using VM-based compartmentalization.

nodes.label: AppVM 1
nodes.description: Example isolated VM containing an email/browser workload in the source's Qubes diagram.

nodes.label: AppVM 2
nodes.description: Example isolated VM containing a password manager in the source's Qubes diagram.

nodes.label: Privileged Instruction
nodes.description: Privileged machine instruction whose handling distinguishes system virtualization from ordinary virtual memory.

nodes.label: Virtual I/O Device
nodes.description: Input/output device exposed to a guest VM.

nodes.label: Memory Overcommitment
nodes.description: Technique for sharing/overcommitting physical memory among VMs.

nodes.label: Kernel Same-page Merging
nodes.description: Technique mapping identical VM memory pages to a shared physical page, especially useful for read-only pages.

nodes.label: Read-only Memory Page
nodes.description: Memory page whose identical contents can be shared safely.

nodes.label: Windows Guest OS
nodes.description: Example guest operating system.

nodes.label: Linux Guest OS
nodes.description: Example guest operating system.

nodes.label: Legacy Operating System
nodes.description: Prior OS versions that can be preserved/rerun through VMs.

nodes.label: Real-time Operating System
nodes.description: Real-time OS that can run concurrently with another complex OS in embedded systems.

nodes.label: Compiler
nodes.description: Compiler producing intermediate representations or machine code.

nodes.label: Compiler Backend
nodes.description: Compiler component that converts an intermediate representation to machine code for a target architecture.

nodes.label: Portable Code
nodes.description: Intermediate code designed to be retargeted to different physical architectures.

nodes.label: Smalltalk

nodes.label: System VM vs Process VM
nodes.description: System VM provides a whole machine/guest OS abstraction; process VM supports a program/process abstraction.

nodes.label: Host vs Guest
nodes.description: Host is the physical machine; guest is the virtual environment executing on it.

nodes.label: Full vs Hardware-Assisted Virtualization
nodes.description: Full virtualization describes the guest-facing virtualization behavior; hardware-assisted virtualization describes architectural support that facilitates the VMM.

nodes.label: System VM vs OS-level Virtualization
nodes.description: System VM can execute a complete guest OS; OS-level environments share the host OS kernel.

nodes.label: VM vs Virtual Memory
nodes.description: Virtual memory abstracts memory; system virtualization generalizes machine abstraction and can include privileged instruction handling.

nodes.label: Snapshot vs Backup
nodes.description: Snapshot is a point-in-time VM state; failover may use backup-server material representing a last coherent state.

nodes.label: Migration vs Failover
nodes.description: Migration deliberately moves a VM to another host; failover continues after host failure using last-known coherent state.

nodes.label: Namespace-style isolation vs VM isolation
nodes.description: OS-level virtualization shares a kernel; system VMs isolate through separate guest environments.

nodes.label: Process VM vs Interpreter
nodes.description: A process VM is the runtime abstraction; an interpreter is one implementation mechanism.

nodes.label: JIT vs Interpreter
nodes.description: JIT is an optimization/compilation technique that can improve process-VM performance; interpreter is an execution mechanism.

nodes.label: Nested vs ordinary virtualization
nodes.description: Nested virtualization places a hypervisor inside another hypervisor; ordinary system virtualization does not require recursive layers.

nodes.label: KSM vs memory overcommitment
nodes.description: KSM merges identical pages; memory overcommitment is the broader memory-sharing/resource-management context.

nodes.label: Virtual disk vs snapshot overlay
nodes.description: Virtual disk is the VM storage abstraction; overlay is a snapshot layer storing subsequent changes.

nodes.label: Guest OS vs host OS
nodes.description: Guest OS executes inside VM; host OS is the surrounding OS when applicable.

nodes.label: Isolation vs Portability
nodes.description: Isolation separates execution environments; process VMs use abstraction to provide platform independence.

nodes.label: Linux Kernel
nodes.description: Kernel through which OS-level virtualization partitions resources.

nodes.label: Debugging
nodes.description: Debugging access cited as an advantage of virtual machines for OS development.

nodes.label: Intel
nodes.description: Processor manufacturer cited for adding virtualization support.

nodes.label: AMD
nodes.description: Processor manufacturer cited for adding virtualization support.

nodes.label: Operating System Development
nodes.description: Development context in which VMs can provide improved debugging access and faster reboots.

relationships.mechanism: System VMs substitute for real machines and execute entire OSs.
Process VMs execute programs in platform-independent environments.
relationships.inverse_or_converse: System VM abstracts a whole machine.

relationships.mechanism: System VM supplies enough machine functionality to execute a complete OS.
relationships.effect: Guest OS executes inside isolated virtual machine.

relationships.mechanism: Hypervisor shares and manages hardware among isolated VM environments.
relationships.effect: Allows multiple guests on one host.

relationships.mechanism: Host is physical machine on which guest VM is emulated.
relationships.effect: Multiple guests may share one host.

equations.name: System VM abstraction
equations.expression: Physical hardware -> Hypervisor -> isolated Guest VM -> Guest OS
equations.meaning: System virtualization substitutes for a real machine and permits an entire OS to execute in an isolated environment.

equations.name: Process VM abstraction
equations.meaning: A process VM runs as a normal host application and abstracts the underlying hardware/OS for one process.

equations.name: OS-level virtualization model
equations.expression: Shared kernel + isolated resource views + resource limits -> isolated OS environments
equations.meaning: OS-level virtualization partitions resources through the kernel while guest environments share the host OS kernel.

equations.name: Snapshot restore model
equations.expression: VM state(t_snapshot) + overlays_after_snapshot -> discard overlays -> restored state
equations.meaning: Restoring a snapshot disregards changes made after the snapshot point and redirects new changes to a new overlay.

equations.name: Migration model
equations.expression: VM snapshot/state + target hypervisor -> resumed VM on target host
equations.meaning: A VM can be stopped/snapshotted/moved/resumed on another host; synchronized snapshots can reduce interruption.

equations.name: Failover model
equations.expression: Host failure + last coherent backup state -> VM continuation
equations.meaning: Failover continues VM operation from the last-known coherent state available to the backup server.

equations.name: Nested virtualization model
equations.expression: Outer hypervisor -> VM -> nested hypervisor -> nested guest VM
equations.meaning: Nested virtualization recursively places hypervisors/VMs inside another virtualization layer.

equations.name: Process VM lifecycle
equations.expression: Process start -> VM creation; process close -> VM deletion
equations.meaning: The process VM exists for the lifetime of its associated process.

equations.name: Same-page memory sharing
equations.expression: Identical read-only VM pages -> one physical page
equations.meaning: KSM can merge identical pages to improve physical-memory efficiency.

equations.name: Full virtualization condition
equations.expression: Simulated hardware sufficient for unmodified guest OS
equations.meaning: Full virtualization permits an unmodified guest OS designed for the same instruction set to run in isolation.

source_claims.claim: A VM virtualizes or emulates a computer system; system VMs execute whole OSs while process VMs execute programs in platform-independent environments.
System VM architecture includes host/guest terminology, historical time-sharing motivations, memory sharing, embedded uses, sandboxing and server consolidation.
Process VMs are host applications supporting one process and provide platform-independent programming environments; cluster-oriented variants abstract communication.
VM history spans 1960s time-sharing, IBM systems, compiler intermediate representations, p-code, Smalltalk, JIT, Self, HotSpot and register-based VMs.
Full virtualization and hardware-assisted virtualization are distinct techniques with IBM, Intel and AMD historical milestones and many implementation examples.
OS-level virtualization partitions resources through the kernel, shares the host OS kernel and includes Docker and container technologies.
Snapshots capture VM state/storage; overlays form a coherent virtual disk; migration moves VM state; failover uses last-known coherent backup state.
Nested virtualization recursively runs hypervisors/VMs and may rely on hardware support such as VMCS shadowing.
VMs are used for security isolation and compartmentalization architectures can limit malware spread.

semantic_distinctions.name: System VM vs Process VM
semantic_distinctions.description: System VM provides a whole machine/guest OS abstraction; process VM supports a program/process abstraction.

semantic_distinctions.name: Host vs Guest
semantic_distinctions.description: Host is the physical machine; guest is the virtual environment executing on it.

semantic_distinctions.name: Full vs Hardware-Assisted Virtualization
semantic_distinctions.description: Full virtualization describes the guest-facing virtualization behavior; hardware-assisted virtualization describes architectural support that facilitates the VMM.

semantic_distinctions.name: System VM vs OS-level Virtualization
semantic_distinctions.description: System VM can execute a complete guest OS; OS-level environments share the host OS kernel.

semantic_distinctions.name: VM vs Virtual Memory
semantic_distinctions.description: Virtual memory abstracts memory; system virtualization generalizes machine abstraction and can include privileged instruction handling.

semantic_distinctions.name: Snapshot vs Backup
semantic_distinctions.description: Snapshot is a point-in-time VM state; failover may use backup-server material representing a last coherent state.

semantic_distinctions.name: Migration vs Failover
semantic_distinctions.description: Migration deliberately moves a VM to another host; failover continues after host failure using last-known coherent state.

semantic_distinctions.name: Namespace-style isolation vs VM isolation
semantic_distinctions.description: OS-level virtualization shares a kernel; system VMs isolate through separate guest environments.

semantic_distinctions.name: Process VM vs Interpreter
semantic_distinctions.description: A process VM is the runtime abstraction; an interpreter is one implementation mechanism.

semantic_distinctions.name: JIT vs Interpreter
semantic_distinctions.description: JIT is an optimization/compilation technique that can improve process-VM performance; interpreter is an execution mechanism.

semantic_distinctions.name: Nested vs ordinary virtualization
semantic_distinctions.description: Nested virtualization places a hypervisor inside another hypervisor; ordinary system virtualization does not require recursive layers.

semantic_distinctions.name: KSM vs memory overcommitment
semantic_distinctions.description: KSM merges identical pages; memory overcommitment is the broader memory-sharing/resource-management context.

semantic_distinctions.name: Virtual disk vs snapshot overlay
semantic_distinctions.description: Virtual disk is the VM storage abstraction; overlay is a snapshot layer storing subsequent changes.

semantic_distinctions.name: Guest OS vs host OS
semantic_distinctions.description: Guest OS executes inside VM; host OS is the surrounding OS when applicable.

semantic_distinctions.name: Isolation vs Portability
semantic_distinctions.description: Isolation separates execution environments; process VMs use abstraction to provide platform independence.

misconceptions.misconception: A virtual machine always means a full guest operating system.
misconceptions.correction: Process VMs execute a single program/process and can exist entirely as a host-OS application.

misconceptions.misconception: System VMs and process VMs are the same abstraction.
misconceptions.correction: They operate at different abstraction levels: whole-machine/OS versus program/process.

misconceptions.misconception: OS-level virtualization creates a separate kernel for every guest.
misconceptions.correction: The source says OS-level guest environments share the host OS kernel.

misconceptions.misconception: Full virtualization requires modifying the guest OS.
misconceptions.correction: The source defines full virtualization as sufficient simulated hardware for an unmodified guest OS.

misconceptions.misconception: Hardware-assisted virtualization is the same thing as full virtualization.
misconceptions.correction: Hardware assistance describes architectural support for the VMM; full virtualization describes the guest-visible virtualization model.

misconceptions.misconception: A snapshot is just a backup copy of one disk file.
misconceptions.correction: Snapshots can include VM storage and other state such as RAM, BIOS and configuration.
Migration intentionally moves state; failover responds to host failure from last coherent backup state.

misconceptions.misconception: Nested virtualization means running containers inside containers.
misconceptions.correction: The source defines it as running VMs/hypervisors inside another virtualization layer.

misconceptions.misconception: Process VMs cannot use JIT compilation.
misconceptions.correction: The source explicitly identifies JIT as an implementation/performance technique for process VMs.

misconceptions.misconception: VMs always hide distributed communication in cluster environments.
misconceptions.correction: The source states cluster-oriented process VMs do not hide that communication takes place.

misconceptions.misconception: KSM and memory overcommitment are identical.
misconceptions.correction: KSM is a specific page-merging mechanism within broader memory sharing/overcommitment.
The source explicitly classifies Docker as an OS-level virtualization example.

why_it_matters.core_problem: Provide abstractions that let software execute as though it has a dedicated computer or portable execution environment while sharing physical computing resources.
why_it_matters.central_model: Physical hardware -> virtualization layer -> isolated system VM/guest OS OR host OS -> process VM -> portable program.
why_it_matters.central_insight: Virtual machines are not one single mechanism. The source distinguishes whole-system virtualization from process-level runtime virtualization and OS-level virtualization, then connects them to hardware assistance, compiler/runtime abstraction, state capture, mobility, resilience and security.
